Scenario 2 Sequence of Events . . . . . . . . . . . . . . . . . . . . . . . . . . . . . . . . . . . 15 1 This report is available at no cost from the National Renewable Energy Laboratory (NREL) at www.nrel.gov/publications 1 Introduction The U.S. power grid faces increasing challenges as data center power demand increases across the country. With artificial intelligence workloads, cloud expansion, and digital transformation driving multi gigawatt interconnection queues, utilities and grid operators are experiencing difficulties in meeting demand. Tradi- tional solutions, such as peak load support plants and transmission upgrades, are often taking longer than expected to complete. Among these constraints, a promising alternative is emerging: flexible demand. A 2025 report by Duke University’s Nicholas Institute [1] estimates that modest curtailment of only 0.25% to 1% of annual con- sumption during critical hours could enable the grid to absorb up to 100 GW of new load without the need for new generation or other major upgrades. Verrus was founded on the belief that data centers can deliver this kind of flexibility—not as a compro- mise to availability, but as a new standard for resilience. The Verrus data center design represents a fundamentally different architectural approach by integrating a grid-aware control plane, a battery energy storage system (BESS), and intelligent power flow optimization across data center campuses. Rather than relying on diesel generators to provide grid relief, this design leverages BESS for firm dispatch to the grid that can be relied upon for resource adequacy planning. Not only do BESS enable meaningful load reduc- tions during times of utility duress, but also they can do so with faster response times than conventional diesel-based systems, providing an additional element of grid stability. This report introduces Vulcan, a 70-MW grid-interactive data center test platform developed in collab- oration with the National Renewable Energy Laboratory (NREL) and powered by NREL’s Advanced Research on Integrated Energy Systems (ARIES) virtual emulation environment.
